full_judgment:
5. After conclusion of the prosecution evidence both the accused appellants were examined under section 342 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and their statements were accordingly recorded. They again pleaded not guilty and declined to adduce any witness in support of their defence. The learned Special Tribunal Judge after completion of the trial convicted and sentenced the accused appellants as aforesaid. 

 6. Let us now discuss the evidence on record in minute details. 

 17. These are all the evidences available on record. 

 18. Mr Ashif Hasan, the learned Counsel appearing on behalf of the accused appellant in Criminal Appeal No. 1381 of 2002 and Mr Md Sharafatullah, the learned Counsel appearing on behalf of the accused appellant in Criminal Appeal No. 1396 of 2002, after taking us through the judgment of conviction and sentence and evidence on record have commonly submitted that out of 12 witnesses examined by the prosecution 6 witnesses are police personnel and the rest are public witnesses and the public witnesses could not prove the case while the police personnel admittedly, proved the case. It is probable that they would be otherwise interested and partisan and, as such, their evidence cannot be relied upon and accepted in the facts and circumstances of the present case. Next, they submit that the 3 seizure list witnesses did not at all support the prosecution case making the same highly improbable and disbelievable. Their third submission is that the occurrence took place in the house of Yousuf Malitha and as Yousuf Malitha and his sons and daughter were present in the house the prosecution should have examined all of them as well as all the inmates of the house for ascertaining the involvement of the accused appellants as regard the recovery of arms and ammunition from their possession. Their another contention is that the mandatory provision of section 103 of the Code of Criminal Procedure being not complied with in the instant case with regard to search, the prosecution case cannot be accepted on that score also. 

 19. Mr Rabiul Karim, the learned Assistant Attorney-General appearing for the State, on the other hand, submits that in the present case prosecution successfully proved beyond all shadow of doubt that the alleged recovery of arms and ammunition was made from the possession of the accused appellants Md Asadul Hossain and Mukul Hossain. The learned Assistant Attorney-General next submits that the submission made by the learned Counsels for the accused appellants to the effect that the evidence of the police personnel cannot be taken into consideration for coming to a decision in connection with 'the instant case has no legs to stand in that it is not rationale to disbelieve the .testimony of the police personnel simply because they belonged to police force, The learned Assistant Attorney-General also submits that even if the public seizure list witness does not support the prosecution case, in spite of that there is no legal bar in convicting the appellants on the unimpeachable evidence of police personnel. In support of his contention, the learned Assistant Attorney-General relied on the decision reported in 6 BLC 113 (SM Kamal vs State). He also referred to another decision reported in 51 DLR (AD) 83 on the point of 'Joint Possession'. 

 20. Be that as it may; we have carefully considered the submission of the learned Advocates for both the sides minutely and gone through the impugned judgment and order of conviction and sentence and evidence on record. We have categorically considered the depositions of all the PWs in support of the prosecution case. After considering the depositions of the witnesses and evidence available on record we are of the view that the learned Special Tribunal Judge arrived at a decision which is based on sound reasoning and in proper appreciation of the evidence on record. To address the first contention of the learned Counsels for both the appellants that the police witnesses cannot be relied upon in convicting a person under section 19(f) and 19A of the Arms Act, we are of the view that it is bereft of any legal consideration whatsoever. In the instant case, all the police personnel namely, PW 1 Md Mosharraf Hossain, PW 4 Sree Nirmal Kumar Roy, PW 5 Md Abu Bakar, PW 6 Sree Dinesh Chandra Biswas PW 9 Imrazul Islam, PW 10 Soumitra Chakma and PW 12 Md Nazrul Islam who is the Investigating Officer categorically and in one voice supported the prosecution case as regard the alleged recovery of arms and ammunition from the possession of the accused appellants to the hilt and thus proved the occurrence as depicted in the first information report in a vivid manner. All these witnesses were cross-examined at length by the defence from where nothing could be revealed so as to demolish the prosecution case or to say more precisely to give another dimension in not believing the prosecution cue of alleged recovery of arms and ammunition from the possession of the accused appellants. The police personnel have given consistent statements as to how the alleged recovery was made after apprehending the accused appellants from the place of occurrence. They have given a graphic description of the alleged recovery and nothing could be revealed from their evidence that they were interested or inimically disposed towards the convict appellants. There is no reason why the evidence of the police personnel should be discarded simply because they belonged to police force. They came before the court and testified to the occurrence. They were fully cross-examined. Their evidence is also evidence within the meaning of section 3 of the Evidence Act. So the unimpeachable evidence of the personnel can very well form the basis of conviction which is a settled principle of law. Regarding second submissions of the learned Counsels that the public witnesses and the seizure list witnesses did not support the prosecution case, the settled principle as it has been submitted by the learned Assistant Attorney-General of which we also hold the same view that even if the seizure list witness does not support the prosecution case the conviction and sentence under section 19A and 19(f) can be given solely on the testimony of the police personnel. We also find support in this regard from the decision of SM Kamal vs State reported in 6 BLC 113 which held that though the other public seizure list witnesses did not support the prosecution case, in spite of that there is no legal bar to convict the appellant on the unimpeachable evidence of the police. 

 This statement of PW 3 gives a clear picture of the situation prevailing at that time from which it can be perceived that the whole area was troublesome with the presence of terrorists group at the relevant time. So, from the evidence of the PW 3, who is a seizure list witness, it can be said that rather it supports the prosecution case indirectly by expressing the prevailing situation of that time which is very much pertinent in this context. 

 22. We cannot subscribe ourselves to believe that as the owner of the house and his sons and daughter and other inmates of the house were not cited as witnesses in the instant case, the prosecution case has become unbelievable on that score. As we have already discussed earlier that all the witnesses, more precisely to say that the police witnesses, have categorically proved the alleged recovery of arms and ammunition from the possession of the accused appellants by corroborating each other in material particulars which cannot be interfered by this court at this stage. As regard the conviction and sentence of the accused appellant Mukul Hossain, we are of the view that the Special Tribunal Judge committed illegality in convicting the accused appellant Mukul Hossain under section 19A of the Arms Act inasmuch as from the evidence on record it is clearly found that from his possession only a 'Tojdani' with 5 cartridges were recovered and owing to that reason he should have been only convicted under section 19(f) of the Arms Act. 

 23. As regard submissions of the learned Counsel of the appellant that the mandatory provision of section 103 CrPC being not complied with in the instant case with regard to search vitiating the trial, we are of the view that this contention does not hold good in that the compliance of section 103 CrPC was not necessary in the present case as we find that the arms and ammunition were recovered from the accused appellants in a sequence when they tried to hide the arms and ammunition hurriedly beneath the bed sheet and tried to flee away and not in a sequence for search of the house and, as such, the contention of the learned Counsel on that score has no legs to stand. 

 24. On the conspectus of the above discussion and on meticulous perusal of the evidence on record and after thoroughly scanning the evidence on record of the PWs, we are of the view that the conviction and sentence passed by Special Tribunal judge as regard the accused appellant Md Asadul Hossain should be affirmed and the appeal should be dismissed and the conviction and sentence of the accused appellant Mukul Hossain should be allowed in part.
